title: Verbs, objects and complements
subtitle: She closed the door. / The door closed.
summary: Recognise which verbs can drop their object, which need a complement, and which take an object plus a preposition or an adjective.

lesson.heading: Transitive or intransitive
lesson.text: Some verbs work both ways, which lets us focus either on the person or thing **performing** the action, or on the person or thing **affected** by it.

examples.text: I've ripped my shirt. / My shirt has ripped.

lesson.note: Also: begin, bend, break, burn, change, decrease, drop, finish, increase, move, open, shut, start, vary, wake - most of them 'change' verbs.

lesson.heading: Leaving out an obvious object
lesson.text: Some transitive verbs don't need an object at all when the meaning is clear from the context.

examples.text: I often sing (songs) in the shower.

lesson.note: Also: answer, ask, change, cook, dance, drink, drive, eat, fail, park, phone, read, smoke, study, wash, wash up, wave, win, write.

lesson.heading: Verbs that need a complement
lesson.text: A **complement** is a phrase that completes the meaning of a verb, noun or adjective. After some verbs we have to add one - an adverb or a prepositional phrase. Other verbs usually have a complement but can manage without one.

examples.note: we have to say where or how

examples.text: He paused for a few moments. / He paused.

lesson.heading: Verb + preposition + object
lesson.text: Some verbs are always followed by a particular preposition and then an object.

examples.text: We had to **deal with** hundreds of complaints.
I'm sure that blue car **belongs to** Murad.

lesson.note: Also: adhere to, aspire to, culminate in / with, detract from, differentiate between, incline to / towards, specialise in.

lesson.heading: Verb + object + prepositional phrase
lesson.text: Some verbs need an object **and** a prepositional phrase to complete them.
lesson.note: Also: attribute ... to, base ... on / upon, equate ... with, inflict ... on, mistake ... for, regard ... as / with, remind ... of.

lesson.heading: Verb + object + adjective
lesson.text: Some verbs are often followed by an object and then an adjective (or adjective phrase) as the complement.

examples.text: The people of this country will **hold the government responsible**.
Conti **pronounced herself fit** for the match.

lesson.note: Also: assume, believe, consider, declare, find, judge, prove, report, think. After declare, find, pronounce and prove the object is usually a reflexive pronoun.

lesson.heading: Making it less formal
lesson.text: Sentences with an object + adjective complement after these verbs are rather **formal**. Adding **to be** after the object, or using a **that**-clause, makes them less formal.

examples.text: Dr Adams argues that house prices will fall, but other economists **believe the opposite true**.
examples.note: less formally ... believe the opposite to be true. or ... believe that the opposite is true.

examples.text: She **declared herself satisfied** with the result.
examples.note: less formally She declared herself to be satisfied ... / She declared that she was satisfied ...

lesson.text: When a sentence feels unfinished, the verb is probably asking for a complement: originate in ..., deal with ..., put something somewhere.

exercises.prompt: Can the object at the end of each sentence be left out without changing the meaning?
categories: The object can be left out

items.text: I called you earlier, but nobody answered the phone.
At about seven Aya washed herself.
Aya parked her car on the drive.
I forgot to mention her when I spoke to you earlier.
Aya helped wash up the dishes.
Aya enjoyed the evening very much.

exercises.explanation: originate needs a complement saying where or how something began.

exercises.prompt: Match each verb + preposition with the phrase that completes it.
Electors deserve more from a political party that ___ national leadership.
exercises.explanation: aspire is always followed by to + object.

exercises.prompt: Years of research by Fleming ___ the discovery of penicillin.
exercises.explanation: culminate takes in (or with) before its object.

exercises.prompt: There's a great restaurant by the harbour which ___ seafood.

exercises.statement: I'm sure that blue car belongs.
exercises.explanation: I'm sure that blue car belongs to Murad. belong needs to + object.

exercises.prompt: The team of amateur footballers inflicted a surprise defeat ___ the first division leaders.
exercises.explanation: inflict takes an object + on: inflict a defeat on someone.

exercises.prompt: It was dark and raining and she mistook the black car ___ a taxi.

exercises.statement: Conti pronounced herself fit for the match.
exercises.explanation: Correct. After pronounce the object is usually a reflexive pronoun, followed by an adjective complement.

exercises.prompt: Less formal version: the scientific evidence proved him ___ guilty.
exercises.explanation: Adding to be after the object makes the object + adjective pattern less formal.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to make a rather formal sentence with an object + adjective.
exercises.answer: The people of this country will hold the government responsible
exercises.explanation: hold + object + adjective complement: hold somebody responsible.
